en: (63v/128) Thus, it has been taught that the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*) alone is to be cultivated, and that very same [mind] consists of those three [aspects] through the distinctions of result, cause, and means; such is the extent of the Blessed One’s teaching. As it is said in the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara*: “Wherein the mind is cultivated as inseparable from emptiness and compassion...”

"That very [practice] is indeed the teaching of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. When that alone is cultivated, the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharmas*) are included within it and are not cultivated separately. Alternatively, for the sake of mastery, that [practice] is practiced as surrounded by the aspects of the factors conducive to enlightenment; therefore, he introduces them with the words "Now," and so forth. "Now" (*atha*) means immediately after the teaching of the path. "Enlightenment" (*bodhi*) is the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Its "sides" (*pakṣa*) are those which are favorable to it. The factors conducive to enlightenment are precisely those that belong to the side of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika*).

In this context, those observations (*anudarśana*) by which mindfulness (*smṛti*) is established—through the knowledge of the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of the phenomena of body, speech, mind, and dharmas, by way of their non-connection with unity or plurality—are the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). They have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their intrinsic nature and serve as the causes of mindfulness. Due to the distinction of their objects (*ālambana*), they are fourfold: the application of mindfulness to the body, the application of mindfulness to feelings, the application of mindfulness to the mind, and the application of mindfulness to dharmas. Among these, the internal body consists of the pentad beginning with the eye.

The external body (*bāhiḥkāya*) consists of the fivefold objects, such as form, which are external to one's own body. The internal-external body (*adhyātmabahirdhākāya*) consists of the remaining elements (*bhūta*) and derivative matter (*bhautika*) pertaining to one's own body and so forth. As for sensation (*vedanā*) and the others, their threefold nature is distinguished by their respective objects, the three types of bodies. Sensation is pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant. Mind (*citta*) refers to the cognitions of the five sense-faculties. Mental factors (*dharma*) are the mental concomitants (*caitasika*), which are wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral. "One who contemplates the body and so forth" means one who contemplates the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the body and the other aggregates.

This body is my body; it is permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful—because there is no conceptualization regarding such things as these. And that observation is non-conceptual by way of non-apprehension.

Now, if the knowledge of all phenomena is attained through the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), what is the use of the subsequent factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣika*)? It is not so; for although they are fully understood by way of their true nature (*dharmatā*), the thirty-seven factors are practiced in order to fully understand the specific characteristics of phenomena (*dharmaviśeṣa*) through their aspects such as impermanence and so forth. For this very reason, those belonging to the vehicle of the Śrāvakas take these as their objects of focus through the aspects of impermanence and so on, whereas Bodhisattvas do so by means of the yoga of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*).

Consequently, even emptiness in its aspects of impermanence and so forth becomes an object for these [meditators], and thus the path of the Śrāvakas is also practiced by way of the gateway of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). By the word "also" (*api*), he includes the state of being a mother and a father. Therefore, because of application with respect and continuity, he is "ardent" (*ātāpī*); because of connection with constant observation and clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*), he is "clearly comprehending" (*saṃprajānan*); and because of connection with mindfulness whose nature is non-forgetfulness and which acts as a protector against that which brings about distraction, he is "possessed of mindfulness" (*smṛtimān*).

He states the benefit of these very qualities—vigor, wisdom, and mindfulness—in the passage beginning with "having subdued" (*vinīya*). "Having subdued" means having abandoned. Regarding "the world" (*loka*), it refers to covetousness (*abhidhyā*) or greed for gain, fame, pleasure, and praise among the worldly dharmas; and it refers to dejection (*daurmanasya*) regarding loss, ill-repute, suffering, and blame.

They are called the "right efforts" (*samyakpradhāna*) or the "right abandonments" (*samyakprahāṇa*) because by means of them the mind is correctly exerted, maintained, or set in motion, or because body, speech, and mind are so directed; alternatively, they are so called because by means of them the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are abandoned. These four, which consist in the nature of vigor, follow after the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*). They are as follows: "of those that have not yet arisen," and so forth.

They cause one to fall into the miserable states (*durgati*) by means of various causes for doing harm; and they cause one to perform actions (*karman*) or to produce karmic impressions (*vāsanā*) of a similar nature—thus, by their etymological definition (*nairukta-lakṣaṇa*), they are "evil" (*pāpaka*). They are unwholesome (*akuśala*), consisting of misconduct of body and so forth. Being of the nature of perversion (*viparyāsa-rūpa*), they are defiled (*sāṃkleśika*) factors (*dharma*) that must be abandoned by those seeking liberation, yet they are called *dharmas* because they maintain their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-dhāraṇāt*). One generates desire (*chanda*) through the vigor of armor (*saṃnāha-vīrya*), thinking, "I shall act in this way"; one exerts effort (*vyāyacchati*) through the vigor of application (*prayoga-vīrya*).

One initiates vigor through tireless vigor; one uplifts the mind and correctly applies it through skillful means vigor. Therein, one uplifts and raises the sunken mind, and one correctly applies and withdraws the agitated mind. The wholesome factors—such as the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) and the perfections (*pāramitā*) along with their equipment—are called "dharmas" because they are maintained as things to be adopted by those desiring the welfare of self and others. For the sake of the stability of these arisen [dharmas] within the continuum, there is the path of accumulation (*saṃbhāramārga*).

Cultivation occurs through immeasurable means, such as the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the formless attainments (*ārūpya*), and the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*). On the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*), it consists of repeated practice; on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), it is fulfillment according to the circumstances; and on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) beginning with the "stainless" (*vimala*) stage, it is the bringing to completion of what was not yet complete. According to the circumstances, there is expansion. The compound "repeated cultivation, increase, and vastness" is a collective term qualifying the specific activities of generating and so forth.

The perfection of supernatural power (*ṛddhisampatti*) consists of supramundane qualities such as the masteries (*abhijñā*), the powers (*bala*), the grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*), and so forth. The bases of supernatural power (*ṛddhipāda*) are the causes for the establishment of that power, and they too are fourfold: the concentration of desire (*cchandasamādhi*), the concentration of energy (*vīryasamādhi*), the concentration of mind (*cittasamādhi*), and the concentration of investigation (*mīmāṃsasamādhi*). For instance, when someone, through intense desire alone, stabilizes the mind within by means of the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*), the concentration characterized by one-pointedness of mind arises through the power of devoted application (*satkṛtyaprayoga*).

For someone who is well-engaged in the abandonment of the unwholesome and the production of the wholesome through the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) and vigor; for someone who purifies the mind by means of the signs of tranquility (*śamatha*), exertion (*pragraha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*); and for someone who correctly investigates, thinking, "What subtle unwholesome states are manifesting in me that I should thoroughly examine?"—these are the concentrations of desire (*chanda*) and so forth.

When these have arisen, and when the ten envelopments—torpor, drowsiness, restlessness, regret, envy, avarice, lack of shame, lack of dread, anger, and concealment (which consists in the hiding of evil)—have been distanced, then for the sake of abandoning the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*)—namely, attachment, aversion, pride, ignorance, doubt, the view of a self-identity, the view of grasping at what is beneficial, false view, adherence to views, and adherence to rules and observances—as elucidated in the *Munimatālaṃkāra*... [he practices] again.

For one who initiates vigor through the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), eight formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*) are to be cultivated as the antidotes to the six faults of all meditative concentration (*samādhi*): namely, laziness, loss of the object, lethargy, excitement, non-application, and over-application. These are: faith, aspiration, exertion, pliancy, mindfulness, clear comprehension, volition, and equanimity. Among these, the first four are the antidotes to laziness.

For it is thus: through faith (*śraddhā*), characterized by conviction in the existence, the quality, and the attainability of the virtues of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the practitioner’s aspiration for them arises. From that, diligence (*vīrya*) follows; from that, pliancy (*karmanya*) of body, mind, and phenomena; and from that, laziness (*kausīdya*) is turned away. (Ratnākaraśānti, *Munimatālaṃkāra*)

Mindfulness (*smṛti*) is the antidote to the loss of the object of focus (*ālambana-saṃpramoṣa*). Clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*) is [the antidote] to lethargy (*laya*) and excitement (*auddhatya*), because by means of it those two are discerned. In that regard, there are two causes for the lethargy of the mind: first, *styāna*, characterized by the lack of serviceability (*akarmanyatā*) of the mind due to the onset of heaviness in the body and the mental faculty, which prevents the perception of the object; and second, *middha*, characterized as a factor (*dharma*) opposed to the activity of the five sensory consciousnesses and serving as the cause for the onset of dullness even in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

The nourishers (*āhāra*) of sloth and torpor (*styāna-middha*), however, are fivefold: languor (*tandrī*), delight (*rati*), yawning (*vijṛmbhikā*), lack of moderation in food (*bhakte ’samajñatā*), and mental depression (*cetaso līnatva*). Restlessness (*auddhatya*) is an indicative mark for remorse (*kaukṛtya*); the nourishers of these two are fourfold: thoughts of relatives (*jñātivitarka*), thoughts of one’s country (*janapadavitarka*), thoughts of immortality (*amaravitarka*), and recollection of laughter, play, and amorous dalliance (*hasita-krīḍita-paricāritānusmaraṇa*). Their function (*kṛtya*), moreover, is to cause the non-quiescence of the mind.

At the time of pacifying lethargy and excitement, however, the fault of non-application arises; as its antidote, volition (*cetanā*) should be cultivated. When lethargy and excitement have been pacified and the mind flows spontaneously, then the fault of application arises; as its antidote, equanimity (*upekṣā*) should be cultivated.

Through these eight causes of abandonment, there arises fitness for meditative concentration (*samādhi-karmanyatā*). By means of that, one accomplishes qualities such as the supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*). And here, this is the sequence of calm abiding (*śamatha*): first, the bodhisattva binds the mind to an internal object of focus for concentration; then, by preventing it from going elsewhere, he causes it to proceed in a continuous stream. Since the mind is naturally fickle, when he perceives it has somehow gone elsewhere, he quickly withdraws it.

By making [the object] increasingly subtle, one establishes the mind right there; one delights in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) by seeing the benefits of concentration. All those specific qualities extend even to the Tathāgatas. One pacifies dissatisfaction by seeing the faults of distraction; these include all sufferings, even those of the Avīci hell. One pacifies covetousness, dejection, and so forth in those who have emerged from concentration, just as one does with dissatisfaction.

In this way, by means of these seven methods, one makes the mind free from faults and causes it to flow spontaneously through application. Because of the relish for that spontaneous flow, one holds the mind correctly upon the object by means of both application and spontaneous flow. Thus, when the mind proceeds toward that object with spontaneous flow through volitional effort for as long as desired, then one should know that calm abiding (*śamatha*) has been accomplished.

He explains this very sequence of cultivation, beginning with "desire" (*chanda*) and so forth. It is endowed with the concentration of desire (*chanda-samādhi*) and the formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇa-saṃskāra*). Separation from the afflictions (*kleśa*) is [the result]. Through cultivation comes detachment (*vairāgya*), which is dispassion (*virāga*). It is the cessation of suffering (*duḥkha-nirodha*). Dependent upon that is relinquishment (*vyavasarga*); it is directed toward the renunciation (*utsarga*) of all acquisitions (*upadhi*). When it is excessively grasped, it becomes agitated (*uddhata*).

It is called a faculty (*indriya*) because of its sovereign power (*indana*). When the attainment of sovereignty for the sake of producing the five supramundane dharmas—faith and the others—has occurred, they become faculties. These are the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*), the faculty of vigor (*vīryendriya*), the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*), and the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*). Among these, faith is the firm conviction regarding the truths, the Three Jewels, and the results of karma.

For when one is well-practiced in the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), through the observation of signs and the subsequent arising of excellence, certainty arises regarding the attainment of the Teacher and the Bodhisattvas; thus, conviction (*abhisaṃpratyaya*) is born, which constitutes his faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*). Due to the preeminence of faith, there is a preeminence of energy and the other faculties; from that, the five faculties come into being. He states these [faculties] with the words beginning "he," and so forth.

One has faith in that which belongs to the realm of desire (*kāmāvacara*), is of an unconcentrated stage (*asamāhitabhūmika*), is mundane (*laukika*), and has not yet realized reality (*anadhigatatattva*)—namely, that which is characterized by right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and the conviction in the selflessness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanairātmyādhimokṣa*), and which determines the existence of the next world—by means of the firm conviction (*saṃpratyaya*) in its existence and so forth. The rest is easy to understand.

The faculties themselves, when cultivated, increase in such a way that, because they cannot be overcome by Māra and other adversaries (*vipakṣa*), they acquire the designation "powers" (*bala*) due to their invincibility; thus he says, "the five," and so forth.

Regarding the passage beginning with "therein" (tatra): on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), awakening (*bodhi*) and perfect awakening (*saṃbodhi*) consist in the realization of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtāvabodha*). Its factors are the seven factors of awakening (*saptasaṃbodhyaṅga*). Among them, investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), vigor (*vīrya*), and joy (*prīti*)—these three belong to the side of insight (*vipaśyanā*). Serenity (*prasrabdhi*), concentration (*samādhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) belong to the side of calm (*śamatha*). Mindfulness (*smṛti*) belongs to both. Joy is that mental gladness directed toward that very same object. Concentration is the one-pointedness of the mind upon the object to be examined.

In this context, mindfulness is the factor of reliance (*niśrayāṅga*), because all [the other factors] proceed by relying upon it. The investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) is the factor of essential nature (*svabhāvāṅga*), because it is the very nature of awakening (*bodhi*). Diligence (*vīrya*) is the factor of departure (*niryāṇāṅga*), because through it one reaches the culmination and establishes oneself therein. Joy (*prīti*) is the factor of benefit (*anuśaṃsāṅga*), because it is the happiness of the mind. Serenity (*prasrabdhi*), concentration (*samādhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—these three are the factor of non-affliction (*asaṃkleśāṅga*), in the sense that "by means of which, relying on which, and that which is the absence of affliction."

For pliancy is the antidote to the dysfunctions that are the cause of affliction; therefore, it is the basis for the absence of affliction. Its support is meditative concentration, and its intrinsic nature is equanimity.

Thus, having seen that the afflictions to be abandoned by vision have been abandoned in himself through the acquisition of these factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), he sets forth the cultivation of the Noble Eightfold Path consisting of three groups for the sake of abandoning those [afflictions] to be abandoned by cultivation. It is called the "Noble Eightfold Path" (*āryāṣṭāṅgo mārgaḥ*). The "Noble Ones" (*ārya*) are the practitioners in training (*śaikṣa*); this path is produced by them for the realization of liberation from the afflictions. Therefore, because it consists of eight limbs for the Noble Ones, it is the Noble Eightfold Path.

These limbs belong to one who has emerged from meditative absorption. However, for one who has entered the path (*mārgasamāpanna*), right intention, speech, action, livelihood, and mindfulness do not exist [in their manifest form]. How, then, does the practice of one who has entered the path become eightfold? Because of the attainment of supramundane dharmas, one acquires a corresponding unmanifest (*avijñapti*) state that is untainted (*anāsrava*); by virtue of attaining this, even after having emerged from absorption, one no longer engages in wrong speech and so forth, but instead engages in right speech and so forth.

Therefore, because the effect is metaphorically applied to the cause, it possesses eight factors; otherwise, it would contradict the state of one who has entered the path. And this noble eightfold path is called "brahmacarya" in the Sūtra—the conduct beneficial for the sake of Brahman, which is Nirvāṇa.

And its body is right view, while the remaining requisites are its equipment. Among these, right view, right intention, and right effort constitute the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*). Right speech, right action, and right livelihood constitute the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīla-skandha*). Right mindfulness and right concentration constitute the aggregate of meditative absorption (*samādhi-skandha*). Therein, right view—following from the time of the factors of enlightenment—is the continuous realization of the reality of the selflessness of all phenomena, characterized by the absence of covetousness, ill-will, and wrong view.

Right intention is likewise so called because it establishes awakening; it consists of mental attention directed toward the abandonment of what is to be discarded and the realization of what is to be adopted, as well as a mind that is exclusively wholesome. Right speech is so called because it communicates things as they truly are, and because it involves the state of abstaining from false speech, slander, harsh words, and frivolous chatter.

Right action (*samyakkarmānta*) is that beyond which there is no further activity of body, speech, or mind; it consists in the abstinence from performing, causing others to perform, or rejoicing in the misdeeds of the body known as killing living beings, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct. Right livelihood (*samyagājīva*) is living by means of wealth acquired through righteous methods, due to the abstinence from wrong livelihood such as hypocrisy (*kuhana*), flattery (*lapanā*), and so forth. Right effort (*samyagvyāyāma*) is vigor, an exertion directed toward the accomplishment of the welfare of oneself and others. Right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*) is the non-forgetfulness of the dharmas as they have been realized.

Right concentration consists in making the object and its aspects manifest. Right view, right intention, and right speech constitute the factors for causing others to attain [the goal], because one causes them to attain it through speech that originates from right motivation. The factors for inspiring confidence in others are threefold: right speech, right action, and right livelihood; for by means of these, in due order, confidence arises in the three [virtues]: in wisdom through discourse and the determination of discussion; in ethical discipline through the non-performance of what should not be done; and in livelihood through the practice of a pure way of life.

Regarding "thinning" (*saṃlekha*), it consists of seeking the requisites for life in accordance with the Dharma and in moderation. The members that serve as antidotes to the opposing factors are threefold: right effort, mindfulness, and concentration. For these are, respectively, the antidotes to: (1) the afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned through cultivation; (2) the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) of lethargy and excitement; and (3) the obstacles to mastery (*vibhutva*) consisting of hindrances to the production of the extraordinary qualities (*vaiśeṣikaguṇa*). This is the summary meaning.

He states its explanation, beginning with "In that regard, which... and so forth. "Supramundane" means because it arises on the supramundane path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). "View" refers to superimposition (*samāropa*). For others, there is the superimposition [of the notion] that the self is permanent, all-pervading, transmigrates, is liberated, and so forth. According to each respective system, it is the very self that is expressed by terms such as "sentient being" (*sattva*) through various imagined distinctions. Having thus established the realization of the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), he speaks of the mind of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*) with the words beginning "Neither annihilation... and so forth.

If your birth were eternal, then its intrinsic nature would exist even in a single moment; because of the absence of that [nature] in the second moment, there would be annihilation. As it is said in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* (15.10ab, 11):
"To say 'it exists' is the view of eternalism; to say 'it does not exist' is the view of annihilation."
For that which exists by way of its own nature (*svabhāva*) cannot be non-existent; thus, [the view] is eternalism (*śāśvata*).
To say, "It does not exist now, though it existed previously," is how annihilationism (*āccheda*) proceeds.

"Becoming" (*bhava*) means arising; it refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*) and so forth. "Dissolution" (*vibhava*) means destruction. Both this arising and destruction do not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), according to the reasoning established in the *Madhyamakamañjarī*; therefore, they are merely superimpositions.

In the *Madhyamakamañjarī*, "wholesome" (*kuśala*) refers to security and liberation, because it consists in the cessation of all calamities; it is wholesome in an absolute sense, like health. The truth of the path (*mārgasatya*), however, is wholesome because it is the cause for attaining that [liberation]. As for the truths of suffering and its origin, they are [considered wholesome] among the contaminated (*sāsrava*) because, by virtue of having desirable maturation, they bring about the production of forms resembling their own nature. Non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion, however, are themselves wholesome and are the causes for the arising, abiding, and growth of other wholesome states, like the roots of a tree.

In this context, non-greed (*alobha*) is a phenomenon opposed to craving, characterized by a lack of attachment to objects. Non-hatred (*adveṣa*) is opposed to hostility, characterized by a lack of harshness toward sentient beings. Non-delusion (*amoha*) is opposed to ignorance; it has the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*) and is right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*). As for bodily and vocal actions, they are wholesome because they are originated by non-greed and the other [wholesome roots]. By contrast, greed, hatred, and delusion are unwholesome and are the roots of the unwholesome. Furthermore, all bodily and vocal actions originated by them are unwholesome.

All afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are indeed unwholesome (*akuśala*). However, all afflictions and secondary afflictions belonging to the realms of form (*rūpadhātu*) and formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*), as well as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and the delusion (*moha*) associated with them in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). By the word "as far as" (*yāvat*), whatever other views may exist are indicated. Precisely because of this realization of being devoid of all superimpositions (*samāropa*), there is right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*). By "conceptual constructions" (*saṃkalpaiḥ*) is meant the superimpositions of the pleasant, the unpleasant, and that which is neither; one does not conceptualize, nor does one produce [them].

The aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*) is the training in higher ethics (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*). The aggregate of concentration (*samādhiskandha*) is the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*). The aggregate of wisdom (*prajñāskandha*) is the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*). The aggregate of liberation (*vimuktiskandha*) is the path of one beyond training (*aśaikṣamārga*). The aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśanaskandha*) is the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣī samyagdṛṣṭi*). Tormenting oneself by speech—that is, through verbal action—is due to a defiled state of mind (*kliṣṭacittatva*), both in the present and for the future.

One’s own affliction arises from speaking, reviling, or exposing the faults of others with an afflicted mind for the sake of creating division or for the sake of not being reconciled. It is also the derision of one’s own frivolous chatter (*saṃbhinna-pralāpa*).

For indeed, when one speaks with an afflicted mind—uttering words accompanied by sensual desires, unrighteousness, uselessness, or vulgar pleasures; engaging in socializing, lamentation, singing, or seductive stories; or prattling on about treatises—one laughs at oneself through this lack of discernment; thus it is said by the virtuous.

By means of that [speech] which is free from the fourfold misconduct of speech, there arises non-dual wisdom (*prajñā*) untainted by the conceptual constructions of the distracted mind. Speech connected with that [wisdom] is indeed its correct origination; for both others and oneself enter into it. For some person, while uttering speech, realizes the meaning expressed by it. Black, unwholesome [actions], such as the killing of living beings, have their ripening (*vipāka*) as suffering only within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because karma to be experienced as suffering does not exist elsewhere.

The white is the wholesome, such as giving and so forth. That, moreover, is both with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and without-outflows (*anāsrava*). The with-outflows [wholesome action] has a pleasant ripening (*vipāka*) from the desire realm up to the third dhyāna. From the fourth dhyāna up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), it has a ripening that is neither painful nor pleasant. For they say that the wholesome has a desirable ripening. The without-outflows, however, has the realization of supramundane attainment as its ripening. "White" means appearing white; for example, like the killing of one's aged parents by foolish Persians out of a notion of merit.

In the same way, other actions such as the taking of life performed by barbarians (*mleccha*) and others out of delusion, with the intention of seeking merit, appear to be white; thus they are called "white" in an intentional sense (*ābhiprāyika*), but in reality they are indeed black. Therefore, its maturation (*vipāka*) is black suffering.
[Note: This refers to Persian (*par sig pa*) and other barbarian customs.]

"Black" refers to practices such as malevolent magic (*abhicāra*). For those of unrefined intellect, this appears as if black; thus, it is merely a "blackness" based on false conceit (*ābhimānika*). However, for a compassionate Bodhisattva who practices it, that very act is white. Therefore, it does not result solely in a white maturation (*vipāka*), but is also capable of destroying evil. We shall explain such a case later. Thus, one who relies upon wholesome action (*satkarmapratisaraṇa*) [is so called] because of the performance of the morality of abstention (*nivṛtti-śīla*), the morality of gathering what is wholesome (*kuśala-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the morality of acting for the benefit of sentient beings (*sattvārthakriyā-śīla*).

The "complete exhaustion" (*samyagvisaṃvādaka*) of actions refers to their finality or conclusion. As for the word "that" (*yat*), it means "which. The "qualities" (*guṇāḥ*) are so called because they are cultivated and practiced for the sake of shaking off the defects of the noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*). They are twelvefold: being an alms-food eater (*paiṇḍapātika*), wearing the three robes (*traicīvarika*), eating at a single sitting (*ekāsanika*), not eating after [the meal time] (*paścātkhalubhaktika*), accepting whatever seat is offered (*yāthāsaṃstarika*), remaining in a sitting posture (*naiṣadyika*), dwelling in the open air (*ābhyavakāśika*), dwelling at the foot of a tree (*vṛkṣamūlika*), dwelling in a cemetery (*śmaśānika*), wearing rag-robes (*pāṃsukūlika*), possessing no more than three robes (*nāmatika*), and dwelling in the forest (*āraṇyavāsika*).

The non-abandonment of their resolve to practice; the restraint of bodily deportment regarding robes and so forth through hypocrisy and the desire for gain; flattery for the sake of obtaining a dwelling; and the artful speech arising from the expectation of profit and honor that serves as a pretext for pleasing others—these characterize the state of being a "coercer" (naiṣpeṣikatva) and a "hint-giver" (naimittikatva).

In this context, "extortion" (*naiṣpeṣikatva*) refers to disparaging another person in their very presence out of a desire for gain, saying things such as "this one is wretched," and so forth; it is so called because, as if crushing the other, one acts out of a thirst to procure gain. "Hinting" (*naimittikatva*) is the praising of an object with the desire to obtain much by giving little; for one gives something and offers praise as a pretext for gain. "Proper conduct" (*svācāra*) is the performance of wholesome deeds. "Contentment with one's own gains" is the state of being satisfied with what one has acquired, free from attachment and the faults of excessive consumption and the like. "Permissible livelihood" (*anujñātam ājīvanam*) is a way of life that is not characterized by usury and other such improper means.

Exertion (*vyāyāma*) is vigor (*vīrya*). It is "false" when its object is unwholesome (*akuśala-viṣaya*). "Entry" (*avatāra*) refers to the vigor of application (*prayoga-vīrya*), which is well-established upon each step of the path during the stage of application for the cultivation of the path. It is "unshakable" because it is not moved by improper discursive thoughts (*vitarka*) and so forth during the fundamental stage (*maula-avasthā*). It is "straight" (*ṛjukā*) because its object is the reality of non-duality (*advaita-tattva*). It is "not crooked" (*akuṭilā*) because it has not been diverted by a wrong path. For this very reason, it is called "application" (*saṃprayoga*) because one is correctly applied (*samyak prayujyate*) to the Noble Path by means of it.
"Correctness" (*samyaktva*) is the reality established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), namely, the absence of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*); concentration (*samādhi*) is [defined] by that.

Now, one might object: "The cultivation of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣyadharma*) is appropriate only for those belonging to the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who are intent upon *nirvāṇa*, but not for Bodhisattvas. As it is said in the *Āryamañjuśrīparipṛcchārddhiprātihāryamahāyānasūtra*: "Mañjuśrī, in a future time there will be monks who will teach the application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) consisting of the contemplation of the body as impure, up to [the point where they say]: 'This alone is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*')."

This is not a fault. For even Bodhisattvas, because they desire the realization of all phenomena in all their aspects, because they regard the non-apprehension of all phenomena as supreme, and because they act to establish the welfare of all sentient beings, perceive qualities in cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) as if it were *parinirvāṇa*. Yet, because there is no locus for establishing the welfare of sentient beings within *nirvāṇa*, they perceive it as disagreeable as if it were *saṃsāra*. Furthermore, because both *saṃsāra* and *nirvāṇa* are merely the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), they perceive their equality; thus, it is precisely for the sake of discerning the nature of non-apprehension that [they practice].
They cultivate the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣa*). As it is said in the *Bhagavatī Śatasāhasrikā*:
"By way of the non-apprehensibility of the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*)," and so forth.

For them, there occurs only the realization of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*); they do not realize the fruit of stream-entry (*srotaāpattiphala*) or nirvāṇa. Thus it is said in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā*: "Abiding in the factors conducive to enlightenment, one knows: 'This is the time for cultivation; this is the time for realization,'" and so forth.

Therefore, by cultivating the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣa*), one realizes nirvāṇa; one merely practices and perfects those very factors. As it is said in that same sūtra, the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*:

"How, Blessed One, are the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) and so forth to be viewed from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha)? He replied: "Mañjuśrī, when the body is seen as equal to space, this is the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body within the body. When sensation, the mind, and phenomena—whether wholesome or unwholesome—are not perceived, it is thus, Mañjuśrī, that the four foundations of mindfulness are to be viewed from the perspective of ultimate reality."

(86v/174) To whatever extent one perceives all phenomena as being in a state of natural composure or naturally distracted, due to the non-apprehension of any objective referent (*ālambana*), this is right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*). Mañjuśrī, whoever thus correctly contemplates the foundations of mindfulness up to the noble eightfold path, of him I say that he has crossed over to the further shore. Furthermore, by one who desires to fully awaken to the omniscient wisdom endowed with the excellence of all aspects, faith (*adhimukti*) must be cultivated toward these teachings.

For this very reason, it is said that these [perfections] are included within the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*). And that mind of awakening, consisting of wisdom and skillful means, when being cultivated, is twofold: the *praṇidhicitta*, which takes the form of a prayer, thinking, "O, may I fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of the buddhahood of all sentient beings," and the *prasthānacitta*, which takes the form of actual engagement.

In that regard, the mind of aspiration (*praṇidhicitta*) is threefold: 1. That accompanied by zeal (*chanda*), characterized by the desire for the complete awakening to all phenomena, consisting of the cultivation of the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). 2. That accompanied by intention (*āśaya*), characterized by the desire for the practice of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), consisting of the cultivation of the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*). 3. That accompanied by resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*), characterized by the desire for the cultivation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharmas*), and consisting of the cultivation of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).

These three are called the stage of the beginner (*ādikarmika-bhūmi*), the stage of equipment (*saṃbhāra-bhūmi*), the path of equipment (*saṃbhāra-mārga*), and the roots of virtue conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*). This is because "liberation" refers to its attainment, and [the path] is beneficial for that. The mind of setting forth (*prasthāna-citta*), however, consists of twelve stages. Among these, one is the state of preparation (*prayoga-avasthā*) consisting of the jewels, lotuses, and the perfections (*pāramitā*). Ten consist of the perfection of generosity and so forth; they are the causal states. The final one is the state of fruition (*phala-avasthā*), which is the perfection of adamantine action (*vajra-karma-pāramitā*), the realization of the ultimate limit of excellence.

In that regard, the stage of application is fourfold: *ūṣman* (heat), *mūrdhan* (summit), *kṣānti* (patience), and *agradharma* (supreme mundane dharmas). These are, respectively, so called because they are the precursors to the fire of supramundane non-conceptual gnosis known as the path of seeing—just as fire is seen from the friction of rubbing fire-sticks; because they are the summits of the fluctuating roots of virtue; because they are the endurance (*kṣamaṇa*) of the supreme mundane dharmas; and because they are the foremost of all mundane dharmas. Among these, the first two have the nature of faculties (*indriya*), while the latter two have the nature of powers (*bala*).

And thus, through the attainment of ever-increasing excellence, the preeminent yoga—the application—arises when no obstacle exists; it is closer to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Because it takes the mundane meditations (*laukikadhyāna*) and formless attainments (*ārūpya*) as its objects, it is the mundane path of cultivation (*laukikabhāvanāmārga*) and the wholesome factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). "Penetration" (*nirvedha*) is non-conceptual realization, which is the path of seeing. It is called "conducive to penetration" because it is beneficial for that "partaking" (*bhāga*), which means the attainment (*prāpti*) of it.

In this state, because the yogin’s resolve (*adhimukti*) is predominant and because this stage serves as the foundation for qualities, it is established as the "Stage of Practice through Resolute Belief" (*sāsravādhimukticaryābhūmi*). Furthermore, these four productions of the thought of awakening (*cittotpāda*), consisting of aspiration, intention, superior intention, and application, are conventional, relative, and mundane. The subsequent productions of the thought of awakening, which seek the perfections (*pāramitā*), are supramundane and untainted (*anāsrava*), because they serve as the progressively higher foundations for qualities.

The eleven stages (*bhūmi*) are to be understood as follows: the Joyous (*pramuditā*), the Immaculate (*vimalā*), the Luminous (*prabhākarī*), the Radiant (*arciṣmatī*), the Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā*), the Facing [the Truth] (*abhimukhī*), the Far-Reaching (*dūraṅgamā*), the Immovable (*acalā*), the Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī*), the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*), and the All-Radiant (*samantaprabhā*).

In that regard, at the first production of the thought of enlightenment—which has the nature of the path of seeing and consists of the seven factors of awakening—a bodhisattva possesses a resolute intention of faith because of the abandonment of all afflictions. Since he has not previously seen the reality of this [path] throughout beginningless saṃsāra, he gives with the intent of worshiping those who have attained final nirvāṇa and others who accomplish the welfare of self and others; whereas for others, it is given out of a desire to benefit the sense faculties and the primary elements. That by which there arises a mind that relinquishes one's own ownership and takes up the ownership of another is "giving" (*dāna*), characterized in this way.

Because it is characterized by an abundance of the perfections of the gift of Dharma, material goods, and fearlessness, and because it is inexhaustible even while satisfying infinite sentient beings, it is "Joyful"; therefore, this is called the Joyful Ground (*pramuditā bhūmi*).

The stages following that consist of the nature of the Noble Eightfold Path. Therein, because one does not tolerate the afflictions through the application of non-regret and joy arising from the engagement in benefiting oneself and others, or because the fire of regret in the mind is extinguished by the abstention from the ten unwholesome actions, the mind is "cool"—this is *śīla*. Due to the preponderance of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), characterized by restraint, the gathering of virtuous dharmas, and acting for the welfare of sentient beings, it is free from the stain of immorality; therefore, it is called *Vimalā* (the Stainless).

Because in this [stage], due to the excellence of the perfection of patience—characterized by threefold endurance through the distinctions of patience that endures injury from others, patience regarding the suffering of [voluntary] ascetic practice, and patience consisting in the contemplation of dharmas—and because it is unshakeable by the occurrence of all undesirable events, it is supported by non-falling samādhi; therefore, there is a great radiance of Dharma, and for that reason, it is called Prabhākarī (The Radiant).

Because in this [stage], due to the preponderance of the perfection of vigor—characterized by a threefold enthusiasm consisting of the continuous accumulation of the wholesome dharmas of body, speech, and mind, the pursuit of the welfare of sentient beings, and the purification of the buddha-field—the fuel of afflictions is burned by the factors conducive to awakening; therefore, it is called Arciṣmatī (The Radiant) because of the arising of the flames of gnosis.

Because in this [ground], due to the absence of any superiority in the roots of all dharmas, there is an excellence of the threefold perfection of meditation characterized by the removal of faults, the state of being conducive to liberation, and sovereign power; and because, despite being unshakable through non-distraction from the focal object, mastery is difficult to achieve due to the mutual opposition between mundane and supramundane knowledge of the sciences and truths; and because even by Māras residing in all world-systems, a bodhisattva cannot be defeated—therefore, it is called "Very Difficult to Conquer" (Sudurjayā).

Because in this [stage], the mind—which is non-abiding and inseparable from emptiness and compassion—becomes manifest through the discernment of dependent origination; and because, by means of the excellence of the threefold perfection of wisdom consisting of hearing, reflection, and meditation, it pacifies all afflictive and cognitive obscurations, there arises the dwelling in the perfection of wisdom called the "Gate of Non-attachment. Therefore, it is called Abhimukhī ("The Manifest").

These six perfections exist substantially, but nominally they become ten. For it is the perfection of wisdom itself, when proceeding in specific modes, that receives the designations of the perfections of skillful means (*upāya*), aspiration (*praṇidhi*), power (*bala*), and knowledge (*jñāna*). Thus, the perfection of skillful means is characterized by the correct dedication of the roots of virtue accumulated through the six perfections toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment; by the removal of one's own faults; by the introduction of sentient beings to their welfare; and by the characteristic of swiftly attaining manifest awakening. This is because, by means of that skillful means, those roots of virtue are rendered inexhaustible.

The perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*) consists of incalculable aspirations, foremost among which are the ten great aspirations; it is threefold by way of its characteristics: that which establishes the continuity of the accumulations, that which follows after the welfare of sentient beings, and that which purifies the buddha-field, through which one practices the six perfections in every birth. The perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*) consists of the power of cultivation and the power of analytical discernment.

The perfection of wisdom (*jñānapāramitā*) is the thorough comprehension of the Mahāyāna according to its intended meaning rather than its literal expression; it is threefold, distinguished by the characteristics of turning back karma (93r/187), removing afflictions (*kleśa*), and turning back Māras and adversaries. It is threefold, distinguished by the characteristics of awakening to the equality of non-conceptualization and conceptualization, and the direct perception of the means for the welfare of sentient beings. It is practiced daily or moment by moment in these three ways, according to one’s intention.

In that regard, because she is endowed with the inexhaustible immeasurables characterized by loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity through the perfection of skillful means (*upāyapāramitā*), she does not abandon the welfare of sentient beings in any state whatsoever; since, in this [stage], the signless dwelling (*nirnimittavihāra*)—which takes the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣa*), the truths, and dependent origination as its object—is carried forward with effort, it is therefore called *Dūraṅgamā* (Far-Reaching).

Because, in this [stage], through the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhānapāramitā*), the fruit is successfully accomplished according to one's aspiration, the signless dwelling—which takes the factors conducive to awakening, the truths, and dependent origination as its object—is effortless and thus immovable; therefore, it is called *Acalā* (Immovable).

Because in this [ground] the Bodhisattva is excellent (*sādhu*) due to the maturation of beings to be trained through the perfections of power (*balapāramitā*) and the inexhaustible means of attraction— generosity, pleasant speech, purposeful conduct, and consistency— and because he is a preacher of the Dharma through the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of phenomena, meaning, etymological interpretation, and eloquence, it is therefore called Sādhumatī (The Excellent Intelligence).

Because in this [stage] the Bodhisattva is consecrated in the dharmas for the sake of the position of crown prince (yauvarājya), it is therefore called Dharmameghā. [The suffix] *ghan* is used in the sense of "sprinkling" (*miha secane*); the change to *ghatva* occurs in the name. Because, through the perfection of gnosis (*jñānapāramitā*) and the inexhaustible analytical knowledges (*pratisamvid*), he teaches the Dharma that wins over those to be trained, he rains down all dharmas effortlessly like a great cloud. And it is called Dharmameghā because, through the sequence beginning with the Tuṣita heaven, it causes the increase of the world's virtue.

Because, through the abandonment of the afflictive and cognitive obscurations along with their residual habitual tendencies within this [state], it consists of the five wisdoms of ultimate purity—such as the mirror-like wisdom—and thus possesses a radiance that illuminates, in every respect and down to each atom, all things throughout the three realms without end, including minds and non-minds, in accordance with the perfection of the realization of the non-duality of compassion and wisdom and the dharmadhātu; in accordance with the equality of selflessness as it truly is; in accordance with the mental activities of sentient beings; and in accordance with the duties to be performed for the world.

Therefore, Samantaprabhā—whose other names are Dharmakāya-svabhāva-mahāsukha-uttama and so forth—is the primary Prajñāpāramitā. It is the state of fruition of all the bodhisattva stages ending with the Dharmameghā, which is adorned by all the pāramitās and is the eleventh stage, the Buddha-stage (buddhabhūmi).

There are eleven stages, or twelve including the stage of conduct through aspiration (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*); or thirteen together with the stage of the beginner (*ādikārmikabhūmi*). Alternatively, there are twelve together with the incomparable stage in the form of the path of distinction (*viśeṣamārga*); or thirteen together with the stage of possessing knowledge (*jñānavatībhūmi*), which consists of the immediate path (*ānantaryamārga*) of the Buddha-stage. Such are the systematic arrangements in the Sūtras, Tantras, and so forth, according to the inclinations of those to be trained.

And upon these stages (*bhūmi*), according to their respective natures and as appropriate, within the successive mental states that follow one another, there are obtained heaps of jewel-like qualities—such as the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) of the divine eye, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, and recollection of former abodes—distinguished by degrees of gradual arising, excellence, and intensity. For a detailed understanding of these, the *Munimatālaṃkāra* is the source.

Bringing all of this together within [the text], he says: "These very [states]," and so forth. The particle *tu* indicates a distinction. Because they are untainted (*anāsrava*), the [four immeasurables] such as joy (*muditā*) are supramundane (*lokottara*). The two stages of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*) are tainted (*sāsrava*); they are not mentioned here as causes because they are easily understood. That in which everything dissolves and becomes connected through identity on all sides is the *ālaya*.

For Kṣitigarbha and the others, as well as all the Buddhas such as Vairocana, have as their very nature joy (*muditā*) and the other [immeasurables], and possess the essential form of the untainted faculties (*indriya*) beginning with faith, or the essential form of the untainted eyes (*cakṣus*) and so forth; they consist of the five untainted aggregates (*skandha*) of form and the rest, and the five wisdoms (*jñāna*) beginning with the mirror-like wisdom. "Specifically" means that these constitute the ground of the fruit (*phalabhūmi*), which is their *ālaya*. Alternatively, *ālaya* means the support (*āśraya*), because each preceding ground serves as the cause for each subsequent one. He clarifies this very point with the words beginning "of the Buddhas. They are "conducive" (*āvāhikāḥ*), meaning they bring about attainment; "supreme" (*parāḥ*), meaning superior to the grounds of the Śrāvakas and others.

[Objection: But in that case, there would be complete identity with the Pāramitānaya. [Response: It is not so, because the stage of Vajradhara, whose nature is great bliss (*mahāsukha*), is established right here. [Objection: But isn't that very stage of the form of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) and so forth? What then is the distinction? [Response: There is a distinction. It is precisely the establishment of its being of such a nature. For example, although the powers (*bala*), the grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*), and so forth—which in reality have the single flavor of emptiness—are taught in the Śrāvaka system, emptiness itself is not established therein, whereas it is established in the Pāramitānaya; thus, a great distinction is proclaimed.

But surely, even for one who has attained the first dhyāna, bliss (*sukha*) is taught, just as in the case of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*). How much more so, then, upon the realization of both forms of selflessness? For indeed, the first stage (*bhūmi*) is called "The Joyous" (*pramuditā*) precisely because of the abundance of joy. True; however, this is not innate bliss (*sahaja-sukha*). For that very reason, it is not great bliss (*mahāsukha*), nor is it the means [to it] during the stage of a beginner. Indeed, a mere pinhole does not experience equality with space simply by being called a "hole."

Now, was it not stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā* that there is the bliss of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment? This has indeed been stated, but the means (*upāya*) for it has not been shown, because the innate great bliss (*sahaja-mahāsukha*), which serves as that means, has not been taught. Therefore, that too must be understood through this very sequence. And so it is said in the *Vairocanābhisambodhi*:
"Behold, O son of good family, your own mind in the form of the moon," and so forth.

Is it then that there is no awakening through the *pāramitā* method? Not at all; for without the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), how could there even be a scent of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening? However, it is said that even at the very limit [of practice], one must necessarily rely upon this single means (*upāya*). Just as the Lord of the Śākyas, seated at the foot of the Bodhi tree at midnight to attain awakening, relied upon the consecration of wisdom (*prajñābhiṣeka*) bestowed by the Perfectly Awakened Ones residing in the sky.

And just as this very Blessed One bestowed the consecration upon Tilottamā, [saying] "Vajragarbha"—enough with excessive detail; those who have understood the oral instructions will clearly recognize this distinction.

To explain how these carry one to Buddhahood, he says: "The thirty-two. These are the channels (*nāḍī*) [of the body], through the meditative resolve (*adhimokṣa*) upon the deities of the arisen maṇḍala as will be described in the third section of the sixth [chapter]. Having removed ordinary ego-grasping, by means of any one of the sixfold yoga—the innate (*sahaja*), suchness (*tathatā*), or action (*karman*)—one practices according to the guru’s instruction. Through the cultivation of the bodhicitta consisting of wisdom and skillful means, which is non-dual in its conventional and ultimate aspects, when they are filled by that conventional bodhicitta, [then one attains Buddhahood].

There is no interval or separation immediately following that state of fullness (*pūrṇatā*). For at that very moment, the state of the fruit—the nature of the ultimate bodhicitta—consists of the sense faculties and so forth as Vajradhara.

However, the status of being Vajradhara does not consist of this alone; rather, for the sake of realizing the innate reality (*sahaja-tattva*), one must rely upon a consort (*mudrā*). For in the thirty-seventh [chapter], it will be established as a rule that the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā occurs together with the consort. And this being the case, [the text says] "in one's own body indeed," and so forth. Is it thought that Buddhahood exists elsewhere as well? It does exist: among the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
For they describe Buddhahood as the eternal Nirvana, the unconditioned state without remainder of substrate, which is to be attained upon the cessation of the five aggregates.

It reveals the nature of the sense faculties and so forth as being the Holder of the Vajra (*vajradhara*). Regarding the passage beginning with "residing within one's own body" (*svadehastham*): it is said to reside within one's own body because it exists without being distinct from one's own body. It is great gnosis (*mahājñāna*) by virtue of being the root of all phenomena (*sarvadharmakanda*). It is free from all conceptual constructions (*saṃkalpa*) by virtue of being great bliss (*mahāsukha*) whose single flavor is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). It is pervasive of all things; this expresses the clarity of great bliss through its uninterrupted experience everywhere, just as [moisture is present] in the waves of water. For this very reason, he says: (100r/201) *svadehastham ityādi*. Because it exists without being separate from one’s own body, it is "residing within one’s own body. It is "great gnosis" because it is the root of all phenomena. It is "devoid of all conceptualization" because it is great bliss whose single flavor is emptiness. It is "pervasive of all entities" because it experiences [bliss] everywhere without interruption; this speaks of the manifest clarity of great bliss, just as [water is present] in the waves. Therefore, he says:

"Though residing in the body, he is not born of the body," because the body arises as having that very [consciousness] as its sole essence, just as a wave [arises] from water. Even if the Lord of the Mandala, together with the deities of the mandala, is known by virtue of pervading all things in this manner, one nevertheless asks in order to know him specifically through the individual deities of the mandala; thus begins the passage starting with "the body. Desiring to indicate the nature of the channels both generally and specifically, he first states their number.

"One hundred and one, increased by two tens" means increased by twenty. He speaks generally: "by way of the division of the four wheels (*cakra*). This refers to the division of sixty-four, eight, sixteen, and thirty-two channels (*nāḍī*) belonging respectively to the wheels of emanation (*nirmāṇa*), dharma, enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*), and great bliss (*mahāsukha*). He speaks specifically: "in the form of the *bodhicitta*. For the *bodhicitta* itself is one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*), since it flows there in abundance. Thus, in the *Dvikalpa*, that is, the *Hevajratantra*, it is said: "The thirty-two [channels] carrying the *bodhicitta* flow into the place of great bliss."

Hṛṣṭā has a joyful face. In the reading *kṛṣṇā*, there is another name, *kṛṣṇavadanā*, as found in another tantra. Varṇā is Rūpiṇī. Caṇḍākī is Caṇḍikā. The divinity and the functions of these channels will be explained later. Having thus listed the channels, he asks about their ultimate nature once they have been known, beginning with the words "etā" (these). The three existences (*tribhava*) are body, speech, and mind; [alternatively] semen, blood, and consciousness. As he will state:

Since *sattva* is the body, *rajas* is speech, and *tamas* is the nature of the mind; since *sattva* is semen (*śukra*), *rajas* is blood (*rakta*), and *tamas* is indeed their origin, they have evolved from those [elements] into those respective forms. Among them, *avadhūtī* is primarily evolved into the form of the mind because it carries the mind; this is the intermediate classification. *Lalanā* is [evolved] into the form of the body because it carries the body, and *rasanā* into the form of speech. Furthermore, because they carry the wind that is the source of speech, both *lalanā* and *rasanā* are also [evolved] into the form of speech.

Others [of the channels] are called "body" because they carry the body; thus, all these [channels], being of such a nature, are devoid of subject and object (*grāhya-grāhaka*), have a non-conceptual (*niṣprapañca*) essential nature, and are of a single flavor with emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Even so, it is specifically established that the *avadhūtī* is free from subject and object, because it is the basis for the arising of non-conceptual great bliss (*mahāsukha*). And so it is said in the *Hevajratantra* (I.i):
"The *avadhūtī*, however, in the middle region, is devoid of subject and object."

(102v/206) Thus, having established both the nature of emptiness and the nature of skillful means, it has been shown that, in the ultimate sense, their equality consists precisely in the *bodhicitta* that is indivisible from emptiness and compassion. This has been briefly indicated; it will be clarified in detail within the exposition of the Arisen Maṇḍala. That *bodhicitta* which enters into the state of fruition is such by virtue of the *bodhicitta* whose essence is the path. The collection of texts that expresses this is likewise so called. A "treatise" (*prakaraṇa*) is that by which illumination is effected through mere enumeration.
Thus ends the second cluster in the *Āmnāyamañjarī* composed by the scholar Abhayākaragupta.
